claims.text: Nitrogen doping will create a Pt-rich surface on a nitrogen-enriched high-entropy-alloy core.
Nitrogen doping optimizes adsorption energies by tailoring the catalyst's electronic structure.
Nitrogen doping produces multiple robust metal–nitrogen bonds.
The metal–nitrogen bonds improve the corrosion resistance of transition metals.
Nitrogen doping and metal–nitrogen bonding suppress metal leaching.
Nitrogen doping suppresses activity loss during low-temperature, transient automotive-exhaust exposure.
The starting material is a nearly equiatomic, multi-element automotive alloy catalyst.
The starting catalyst has low platinum content.
Nitrogen doping can be applied through gas-phase exposure or chemical treatment.
A Pt-rich surface layer and metal–nitrogen bonds stabilize the alloy structure.
Optimized adsorption energies will improve conversion of automotive exhaust pollutants.
Compared with the untreated catalyst, the nitrogen-doped catalyst will have greater catalytic activity under transient, low-temperature H2O/NO exposure.
Compared with the untreated catalyst, the nitrogen-doped catalyst will have greater durability after H2O/NO exposure and thermal aging.
The predicted benefits apply under low-temperature, transient conditions typical of gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust.
The benefits may not extrapolate to high-temperature or excessively contaminated environments.
Related electrocatalysis evidence shows improved activity and stability for a nitrogen-doped Pt-rich-shell/PtCoFeNiCu-core high-entropy-alloy catalyst.
The magnitude and long-term performance of the proposed effect under real automotive-exhaust conditions remain unquantified.
A controlled comparison of nitrogen-doped and untreated catalysts under transient exhaust exposure and thermal aging can test the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both activity and durability relative to the untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.
